note.explanation: An enzyme acts on a substrate at its active site. In the lock-and-key model, the active site has a fixed structure. In the induced fit model, the active site changes shape when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
examples: Lock-and-key: a substrate fits into a fixed active site.
Induced fit: the active site reshapes when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
note.checkAnswer: The lock-and-key model has a fixed active site; in the induced fit model, the active site is reshaped.
note.simple: The active site is the part of an enzyme where the substrate fits and the reaction happens. The two models explain whether that site stays fixed or changes shape.
note.checkQuestion: In which model is the active site reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme?

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the lock-and-key model?
rationales: Correct: the model describes a fixed active site into which the substrate fits precisely.
Incorrect: reshaping of the active site describes the induced fit model.
Incorrect: the substrate interacts with the enzyme to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
Incorrect: the substrate is transformed into product or products; it does not become the enzyme.

options: The active site has a fixed structure.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the induced fit model?
rationales: Incorrect: a fixed active site is the feature of the lock-and-key model.
Correct: in the induced fit model, the active site is not rigid and is reshaped during interaction with the substrate.
Incorrect: the model describes the substrate interacting with the enzyme, not the product binding first.
Incorrect: this section does not describe the enzyme as being consumed.

rationales: Correct: the substrate and enzyme form an enzyme-substrate complex.
Incorrect: the active site is part of the enzyme and is present before the complex forms.
Incorrect: the product is formed after the enzyme catalyzes the reaction.

It changes the product back into the substrate.

rationales: Correct: the enzyme catalyzes the reaction, transforming the substrate into product or products.
Incorrect: the section describes the substrate being transformed into products, not the reverse.
Incorrect: the products are released from the enzyme.
Incorrect: the enzyme catalyzes the reaction; it does not become the substrate.

written.text: What is the active site of enzyme? State its importance in enzyme specificity.
written.finalAnswer: An active site is a pocket or cleft on the enzyme surface, directly involved in catalysis. Its structure allows a specific substrate to fit and bind, giving the enzyme specificity.

written.text: Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
written.finalAnswer: The lock-and-key model has a fixed active site into which the substrate fits precisely. In the induced fit model, the active site is not rigid and is reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme. In both models, an enzyme-substrate complex forms, the enzyme catalyzes the reaction, and product or products are released.

example.question: Describe the sequence of events in the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.
example.answer: The enzyme has a fixed active site. The substrate fits precisely into it to form an enzyme-substrate complex. The enzyme catalyzes the reaction, transforming the substrate into product or products, which are released from the enzyme.

explain.title: The active site
explain.body: An enzyme has one or more pockets or clefts on its surface. These are called active sites. The active sites are directly involved in catalysis.

explain.title: Lock-and-key model
explain.body: This model was proposed by a German chemist Emil Fischer in 1894. According to it, the active site of enzyme has a fixed structure. The substrate molecule fits precisely into it to form an enzyme-substrate complex. The enzyme catalyzes the reaction and substrate is transformed into product/s. Then, the product is released from the enzyme.

explain.title: Induced fit model
explain.body: This model was proposed by an American biologist Daniel Koshland in 1958. According to this model, the active site of enzyme is not rigid. When substrate interacts with the enzyme, its active site is reshaped to perform its function.

explain.title: The key comparison
explain.body: The lock-and-key model has a fixed active site. The induced fit model has an active site that is reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.

mistakes: Do not say that the active site changes shape in the lock-and-key model; it has a fixed structure.
Do not describe the induced fit active site as rigid; it is reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
Do not confuse the substrate with the product: the substrate binds first and is transformed into product or products.
When comparing the models, name the enzyme-substrate complex and explain that the product or products are released.
